To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) iterative learning from positive data is possible for a wide class of recursive languages; (2) bounded negative counterexamples can help iterative learning; (3) arbitrary negative counterexamples are useless for iterative learning; and (4) learners in the iterative learning model can work in a non-U-shaped way.

iterative learners that get all positive examples from a target language, test every new conjecture against a teacher (oracle), and use limited long-term memory, can learn in the limit even without any negative counterexamples, but can do better if they get least negative counterexamples (the ones whose size is less than or equal to the maximum size of positive examples seen so far), and that the iterative learner that uses least counterexamples can be non-U-shaped, never abandoning the first right guess.

(1) bounded counterexamples help a learner to avoid false positives, (2) unbounded counterexamples are not needed for a learner to avoid them, and (3) a learner in the model of iterative learning can never abandon its first conjecture.
